subject: Political Science
title: Paper II - Comparative Political Systems and Global Integration

segments.text: For every comparative-systems topic, start from the formal constitutional or institutional structure, then explain how it actually operates in practice through parties, executives, legislatures, courts, federal arrangements, or decision rules. Comparison is strongest when the same criteria are applied consistently to each system, rather than simply describing each country separately in isolation.

is a federal presidential republic under a written constitution, with separated institutions sharing power: Congress legislates, the president heads the executive, and federal courts exercise judicial functions including constitutional review developed through case law over time. Federalism divides power between federal and state levels; checks and balances deliberately make these institutions interdependent on each other. The

is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy with an uncodified constitution assembled from statutes, common law, conventions, and authoritative practice, rather than one single written constitutional text; parliamentary sovereignty is the classic governing doctrine, though political reality is also shaped by devolution, the courts, rights law, and disciplined party government — the prime minister and cabinet depend continuously on maintaining the confidence of the House of Commons.

’s Fifth Republic combines a directly elected president with a prime minister and government responsible to parliament, making it a semi-presidential system; presidential influence is especially strong when the president and the parliamentary majority align politically, while “cohabitation” (when they do not align) has historically increased the prime minister’s practical role.

is a federal parliamentary republic governed under the Basic Law; the Bundestag is the main elected federal chamber, while the Bundesrat represents the Länder (state) governments specifically in federal legislation, and the Federal Chancellor leads government through parliamentary election, protected by the notable “constructive vote of no confidence” mechanism (a chancellor can only be removed by simultaneously electing a successor, which prevents pure destructive no-confidence votes with no replacement in place).

increases cross-border flows of goods, capital, information, people, and ideas, creating both real interdependence and genuine political backlash; it can constrain some national policy choices while simultaneously giving states new markets, institutions, and tools — politics is what actually determines who gains, who loses, and how the underlying rules get made in the first place.

refers to transnational networks and organizations acting across borders outside formal interstate diplomacy — NGOs, advocacy networks, professional groups, and social movements can shape international norms and agendas, though their accountability, funding sources, and genuine representativeness are all legitimately contested.

is a unique regional integration project in which member states share authority through common institutions and law in specified policy areas; core institutions include the European Council, the Council of the EU, the European Commission, the European Parliament, and the Court of Justice, and integration covers a single market plus, for euro-area members specifically, a shared monetary union, while many competences still remain divided between the EU and individual member states.

is a South Asian regional organization created to promote regional cooperation among its member states; its potential is large given genuine geographic and social links across the region, but political tensions — especially India-Pakistan rivalry — have repeatedly limited high-level cooperation and even basic summit continuity.

links states across West, Central, and South Asia with goals in trade, transport, energy, and broader economic cooperation; its central challenge is turning genuine connectivity potential into actually implemented cross-border trade and infrastructure, given how much member economies and political conditions vary.

are both important international regimes but with genuinely different mandates: the IMF supports monetary and financial cooperation and provides balance-of-payments financing under agreed programmes, while the WTO provides rules and a forum specifically for international trade agreements and trade-dispute processes. Both influence national policy substantially, but through very different channels — criticism of either institution concerns conditionality, representation, available policy space, and unequal bargaining power between members, while supporters stress the value of predictable rules and available financing; the two should never be treated as the same kind of institution simply because both operate internationally.

blocks.text: C. Political Systems of Turkey, Iran, Malaysia, India, and China

segments.text: is a republic with a presidential system following constitutional changes implemented from 2018; the president is both head of state and head of the executive, the Grand National Assembly legislates, and the courts form the judicial branch — contemporary analysis should address party competition, executive power, and institutional checks rather than relying on any single personality.

combines republican elected institutions with Islamic constitutional guardianship structures: the Supreme Leader holds major constitutional powers, the president and parliament (Majles) are elected, and bodies such as the Guardian Council perform important supervisory and constitutional roles — this creates a genuine dual structure of elected and unelected authority operating alongside each other.

is a federal constitutional monarchy and parliamentary democracy; its federal king is selected from among hereditary rulers under a rotating system, while executive government is led by a prime minister who must command parliamentary confidence — federalism, ethnic politics, and shifting coalition competition are all important analytical themes for understanding how Malaysian politics actually functions in practice.

is a federal parliamentary republic under a written constitution; the president is the constitutional head of state, while the prime minister and council of ministers exercise actual executive leadership while remaining responsible to the Lok Sabha (lower house), the Union is federal with notably strong central features compared to many other federations, and the Supreme Court holds constitutional review powers.

, formally the People’s Republic of China, is a socialist state in which the Communist Party of China occupies the leading political role; state institutions include the National People’s Congress, the presidency, the State Council, and the courts and procuratorates, but party institutions — not these formal state bodies alone — are genuinely central to political leadership and personnel control, marking a fundamental structural difference from competitive multiparty systems.

Comparative Political Systems and Global Integration key takeaways: applying the same consistent analytical criteria (constitutional structure, then how it operates in practice) to every system studied is what makes genuine comparison possible, rather than merely describing countries one after another. Presidential (US), parliamentary (UK, Germany), semi-presidential (France), and party-state (China) systems each organize the relationship between executive and legislative power in a genuinely different way. Iran’s theocratic-republican duality and Malaysia’s federal-monarchical-ethnic combination both show how a single system can blend elements not usually found together in standard Western-derived typologies. Globalization and the EU, SAARC, ECO, IMF, and WTO together illustrate that regional and global integration can take very different institutional forms, with correspondingly different degrees of shared authority.
